item.content:encoded:
Two Baldwin County residents are facing drug charges after police say they showed up to court with drugs and a child. Daphne police say 30-year-old Cody Hicks of Bay Minette was seen smoking marijuana in a vehicle outside the courthouse Tuesday. Officers found marijuana and drug paraphernalia near a child’s car seat. Police say the vehicle’s owner, 25-year-old Autumn Barker of Spanish Fort, had methamphetamine in her purse and admitted it was hers. Both were arrested, and the three-year-old child was turned over to a family member.

item.content:encoded:
Pensacola City Councilman Charles Bare has received a Gold Certificate of Excellence from the Florida League of Cities. The program recognizes elected municipal officials for completing training and continuing education. Bare completed the program’s inaugural year, from August 2025 through July 2026, earning points through webinars, ethics training, leadership institutes and other Florida League of Cities events. Bare says continuing education is critical to his ability to serve Pensacola residents.

According to an arrest report, deputies were called to the Santa Rosa County Auditorium on Spikes Way after Marc Manchon was seen recording voters and yelling at them. The report says two citizens told deputies they were scared and…
item.content:encoded:
A Santa Rosa County man is accused of intimidating voters at a polling facility during Tuesday's Primary election. According to an arrest report, deputies were called to the Santa Rosa County Auditorium on Spikes Way after Marc Manchon was seen recording voters and yelling at them. The report says two citizens told deputies they were scared and intimidated while trying to vote. Manchon allegedly pushed a man assisting poll workers and later resisted arrest after refusing to identify himself. He's charged with two counts of voter intimidation or suppression, three counts of disturbing the peace, battery and resisting arrest. He was released on bond Wednesday.

item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- The City of Pensacola is hosting a Workforce Summit on August 26th from 2:30 to 4 p.m. — bringing together more than 30 confirmed attendees including representatives from Pensacola State College, Northwest Florida State College, and Florida Commerce Secretary Kelly. Officials say the summit is timed to coincide with the CareerSource Florida board meeting also being held in Pensacola at UWF the following day — the first time in recent memory that meeting has been held in Northwest Florida rather than South or Central Florida. Officials say the goal is preparing the regional workforce pipeline for the wave of high-paying jobs expected from the Burdon shipbuilding project and related industries — with attendees also touring the American Magic building during their visit.

item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola Yacht Club's women's sailing team has brought home the Knost Championship for the first time since the early 1970s. The team, which included three service academy graduates now training in Naval Aviation locally, won the title August eighth and ninth in Pass Christian, Mississippi. Vice Commodore Susan Domagala says the win connects generations of PYC sailors, spanning back to the club's championship run in 1971 through 1973. The victory adds to Pensacola's growing reputation as a premier sailing hub, following American Magic's new High-Performance Center at the Port of Pensacola.

item.title: Chief Winstrom Talks Flock Cameras — And Why a Trip to a Holocaust Museum Still Shapes How He Thinks About Them
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- PPD Chief Eric Winstrom joined Pensacola's Morning News on Thursday to talk about license plate readers — the same topic that Sheriffs Chip Simmons and Bob Johnson have chimed in on earlier this week. Winstrom brought something new to the conversation — a story from early in his career in Chicago about the…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- PPD Chief Eric Winstrom joined Pensacola's Morning News on Thursday to talk about license plate readers — the same topic that Sheriffs Chip Simmons and Bob Johnson have chimed in on earlier this week. Winstrom brought something new to the conversation — a story from early in his career in Chicago about the effectiveness of the cameras.


When Winstrom got promoted to sergeant there, the department sent every new supervisor to the Holocaust Museum in Skokie, Illinois, for an eight-hour training. He says it didn't make sense to him at the time. Then he sat through it. The training walked through how German police, before the Nazis took power, were a respected, effective department — and how over time they got turned into a tool for rounding up and murdering people. The message to every new supervisor was simple: you have a lot of power, we hold you to a high standard, and you never put yourself in a position where you're helping an evil government do evil things.

Winstrom says that's exactly the fear people should have about powerful tools in the wrong hands — and he doesn't think it's an unreasonable fear at all. But he says the fight isn't with the camera. It's with what kind of government you have. He told Andrew McKay that if you stripped every Flock camera out of the country tomorrow and swapped in a socialist government, you'd have ten times the surveillance within a year — just aimed at different things.


He also pushed back on the groups leading the loudest opposition locally, pointing out that organizations pushing to "abolish police, abolish prisons" also list Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela as regimes they support — countries where AI cameras track women without hijabs, where the government monitors every Google search, where the military runs over protesters. He says that's not an accident, and it makes him skeptical of how sincere the privacy argument really is coming from that direction.


On the numbers, Winstrom says he's seen firsthand what license plate readers can do. As a homicide commander in Chicago, he watched the department's solve rate — which was sitting around 30 percent — roughly double once LPRs came into wide use. He calls it one of the most effective tools law enforcement has picked up in his career.


Winstrom says he's not dismissing anyone's concerns, though. He says he doesn't love facial recognition, doesn't love geofence tracking, doesn't love how much London or China surveil their own people. He grew up on the same dystopian movies and books everybody else did. But he draws a line between that kind of surveillance and what Flock actually does — which he says is just a record of license plates passing a fixed point, with real accountability built in for any officer who misuses it.

Combined with a hundred-million-dollar state investment, the four-hundred-fifty-six-million-dollar effort will upgrade more than nine-hundred rail crossings with new gates, lighting, signage, and…
item.content:encoded:
Florida's Department of Transportation has landed a three-hundred-fifty-six-million-dollar federal grant to overhaul rail crossing safety statewide. Combined with a hundred-million-dollar state investment, the four-hundred-fifty-six-million-dollar effort will upgrade more than nine-hundred rail crossings with new gates, lighting, signage, and pedestrian warning systems. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue calls it a transformational opportunity for rail safety. Crossings with the highest history of incidents will be prioritized first as the work rolls out.

item.content:encoded:
Florida Power and Light now operates one-hundred-twenty solar energy centers across the state, making it the largest utility-scale solar portfolio in the country. The company says solar investments have saved customers more than one-point-three-billion dollars by avoiding fuel costs, with enough capacity now to power over one-and-a-half million homes. F-P-L has also added agrivoltaics projects at several sites, allowing land to be used for both solar production and cattle grazing at the same time.

item.title: Mayor Reeves Reacts to Re-Election Win, Curfew Failure, Veterans Park Restrooms and More
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Mayor D.C. Reeves joined Pensacola's Morning News Wednesday morning fresh off his re-election victory — calling in from school drop-off where he and daughter Caroline were celebrating after a long night of sign-waving at Bayview Park and a victory party. The mayor earned 53 percent of the vote in Tuesday's primary…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Mayor D.C. Reeves joined Pensacola's Morning News Wednesday morning fresh off his re-election victory — calling in from school drop-off where he and daughter Caroline were celebrating after a long night of sign-waving at Bayview Park and a victory party. The mayor earned 53 percent of the vote in Tuesday's primary — defeating five challengers without a runoff and securing a second term without a November race.


The Re-Election

Reeves says the margin told him something important about how Pensacola residents actually feel about their city — and says it is very different from the picture painted on social media. He says decisions are not made in Facebook comment sections — they are made in living rooms when parents are FaceTiming their kids in college and thinking about whether Pensacola is a place they want to come home to. He says the vote tells him the city is going in the right direction and that residents want to keep pushing forward — not tear things down. He was quick to say he knows he can be a better mayor and that the city can always improve — but says acknowledging imperfection and declaring the city broken are two very different things. Reeves first won the mayor's race in 2022 at 38 years old, also without a runoff. The final results — Reeves 53 percent, Alicia Trawick 21 percent, Ann Hill 10 percent, Jermaine Williams 8 percent, Jasmine Brown 4 percent, Eric Shorter 3 percent.


Juvenile Curfew — Coming Back in September

Reeves was visibly frustrated about the juvenile curfew ordinance's failure at city council last week — and said the process leading up to the vote was more troubling than the vote itself. He says his team spent almost two weeks preparing the proposal and that every council member who showed up with last-minute objections had the same two weeks to raise those concerns privately and did not. He called that disrespectful to Police Chief Eric Winstrom — who has been the strongest advocate for the tool — and to the city attorney's office that did the legal work. He singled out Councilman Charles Bare for sending a written opposition document before even hearing from the chief — saying Bare burned the boat before the conversation started. Reeves also addressed the broader pattern of council decisions being driven by Facebook reaction rather than actual engagement with the substance of what is being proposed — saying there is a meaningful difference between showing up at a meeting and actually reading the ordinance you are opposing. The curfew ordinance will be brought back before city council in September. Reeves says he remains open to any conversation about how to improve it — before the meeting, not at the podium.


Land Development Code and Trees

The land development code overhaul that recently cleared city council will be followed up with additional protections for heritage oaks and southern live oaks. Reeves says he and Councilman Jared Moore are developing those additional specifications — which will come as a separate item rather than delay the broader LDC rewrite that had already begun. He says the goal is to make sure the trees the community loves most are genuinely protected going forward.


Veterans Memorial Park Restrooms

The two-bathroom prefab facility at Veterans Memorial Park has been approved by city council and is on track for completion by early 2027. Reeves defended the decision against critics who wanted four bathrooms — noting that only one park in the city's 95-park portfolio has two bathrooms outside of parks with community centers. He also pointed out that even four bathrooms would not be sufficient for major events like Veterans Day and Memorial Day when portable facilities are still needed regardless of what is permanently installed. He says the flood zone restrictions on the site limited options and that the city made the right call given the constraints. He says after 12 years of discussion he is simply looking forward to getting it done.


Second Term Priorities

Reeves says his second term will be defined by getting major projects already in motion across the finish line — specifically Birdon shipbuilding at the port, the $110 million airport terminal expansion, the Reverb development at Maritime Park, the Baptist Hospital site redevelopment, and a possible inland port at the Super Fun site that he says could significantly expand the port's economic development capacity. He says the city is going on offense and does not plan to slow down.

item.title: Primary results for Northwest Florida
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Santa Rosa County Jeff Ates won the Republican primary for Santa Rosa County Commission District 2 , finishing first in a six-candidate field. Ates received 6,073 votes, or 26.40% of the 23,003 ballots cast. He finished 1,592 votes ahead of former Milton City Councilman Jeff Snow, who received 4,481 votes. Reni “Renee” Johnmeyer finished third…
item.content:encoded:
Santa Rosa County

Jeff Ates won the Republican primary for Santa Rosa County Commission District 2, finishing first in a six-candidate field. Ates received 6,073 votes, or 26.40% of the 23,003 ballots cast. He finished 1,592 votes ahead of former Milton City Councilman Jeff Snow, who received 4,481 votes.

Reni “Renee” Johnmeyer finished third with 3,827 votes, followed by Erin Nisewonger with 3,589. Incumbent Kerry Smith finished fifth with 3,425 votes, while RC Pittman received 1,608. Ates will face write-in candidate John Williams in the November 3 election.

Dean Light defeated incumbent Ray Eddington in the Santa Rosa County Commission District 4 race. With all 41 precincts reporting, Light received 14,421 votes, or 51.13%, compared with Eddington's 13,783 votes, or 48.87%. The result continues a trend dating to the 2011 redistricting: according to the information provided, no District 4 incumbent has won reelection since the district lines were redrawn because of growth in southern Santa Rosa County.

Holley-Navarre Fire District voters approved the district's first fee increase in 10 years. The referendum passed 56.71% to 43.29%, with 3,682 voters supporting it and 2,811 opposed. The increase will raise the annual residential fee from about $162 to $231 for homes up to 2,300 square feet, an increase of roughly $5.70 per month.


Escambia and Santa Rosa state races

Jon Fay won the Republican nomination for Florida House District 2. The retired Navy flight officer and former Blue Angels executive officer received 14,642 votes across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties, compared with 4,190 for Trei McMullen. Fay won approximately 79% of the vote in Escambia County and 75% in Santa Rosa County.

Fay will face Democratic nominee Johnny Austin Thompson in November. Thompson is a 25-year-old Washington High School graduate and current Harvard Law student.

Escambia County District 2 Commissioner Mike Kohler also won his Republican primary, defeating Glenn Dorsey. With all but one district reporting, Kohler had 2,998 votes, or 62.41%, while Dorsey had 1,806 votes, or 37.59%.


Escambia County School Board

All three Escambia County School Board incumbents who faced challengers won reelection.

Kevin Adams defeated Erin Toler in District 1 and will serve a third term. Adams had 6,638 votes, or 60.92%, compared with Toler's 4,259 votes, or 39.08%, with 12 of 13 precincts reporting.

In District 2, three-term incumbent Paul Fetsko defeated Gerald Washington. Fetsko had 5,024 votes, or 66.29%, compared with Washington's 2,555 votes, or 33.71%, with 15 of 16 precincts reporting.

David Williams also won a second term in District 3, defeating newcomer Isaac Williams.

Because the school board races are nonpartisan and only two candidates were on the ballot in each race, the primary winners were elected outright rather than advancing to a November runoff.

Voters also overwhelmingly approved a referendum that will restore an elected school superintendent in Escambia County. With 75 of 80 precincts reporting, 36,889 voters, or 71.22%, supported the measure, while 14,905, or 28.78%, opposed it.


Pensacola

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves won reelection outright. With all 20 precincts reporting, Reeves received 53.45% of the vote. Under the city's charter, a candidate who receives more than 50% in the August election wins the office without a runoff.


Statewide and congressional races

Byron Donalds won the Republican nomination for Florida governor, defeating Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, James Fishback and former House Speaker Paul Renner. With nearly 1.4 million votes counted, Donalds had 49%, followed by Collins with 25%, Fishback with 10% and Renner with 8%. The Associated Press called the race shortly after 8 p.m. Eastern.

Congressman Jimmy Patronis won the Republican primary for Florida's 1st Congressional District, with the Associated Press calling the race at 7:17 p.m. Central.

item.title: Florida Primary Election Results: Moody, Donalds Lead Republican Races
item.dc:creator: Robert Rees
item.description: Florida voters cast ballots Tuesday in the state's primary election, determining nominees for U.S. Senate, U.S. House of Representatives, Florida Governor, and numerous state races ahead of November's general election. On the Republican side for governor, Byron Donalds secured a commanding lead with 798,921 votes, or 47.9 percent of the GOP…
item.content:encoded:
Florida voters cast ballots Tuesday in the state's primary election, determining nominees for U.S. Senate, U.S. House of Representatives, Florida Governor, and numerous state races ahead of November's general election.

On the Republican side for governor, Byron Donalds secured a commanding lead with 798,921 votes, or 47.9 percent of the GOP primary vote. Jay Collins finished second with 419,013 votes representing 25.12 percent of the field.

Democrats rallied behind a unified ticket, with the David Jolly and Gwen Graham partnership capturing 746,788 votes, or 61.02 percent of the Democratic primary for governor. The tandem significantly outpaced rival Dayna Marie Foster, who received 184,550 votes.

In the U.S. Senate race, Republican Ashley Moody dominated her primary with a decisive victory, earning 1,296,258 votes for 79.57 percent of GOP voters. Her closest competitor, Chris Gleason, garnered only 223,758 votes.

On the Democratic side, Angie Nixon prevailed with 687,075 votes, representing 55.94 percent of the primary electorate. Alex Vindman came in second with 541,123 votes, or 44.06 percent.

In congressional races across Florida's districts, Republican Jimmy Patronis dominated District 1 with 61,918 votes, claiming 71.19 percent of that primary. In District 5, Republican John H. Rutherford secured victory with 52,977 votes for 67.7 percent of the Republican primary.

Democratic congressional nominee races saw various winners emerge across the state's districts, with candidates like Leela Gray capturing 65.14 percent of the District 13 Democratic primary.

Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time Tuesday, with results released shortly thereafter through the Associated Press. The primary elections set the stage for competitive general election matchups this November across multiple statewide and congressional races that will shape Florida's political landscape.
